title: How robot arms get the data they need to move
lead: Einsia’s training environments let robot software act on simulated objects. Universal Robots and Inbolt have moved part localisation to the robot’s own controller.

news.title: Einsia releases a simulator with 10,807 robot tasks
news.summary: Singapore’s Einsia AI released RoboUniverse-10K, an open set of simulated environments for training robots. One model improved from 0.8% to 21.2% success after additional training, measured on a separate set of 500 tasks.
news.details: Singapore lab Einsia AI released RoboUniverse-10K on November 25. It is a set of computer environments in which a program can move a robot arm and change the state of objects. The researchers tested whether extra training in these environments could help a model complete new tasks. On a separate set of 500 tasks, their model's success rate rose from 0.8% to 21.2% after training.
news.technical_novelty: The developers turned recordings of real robots into interactive environments that can check the final result.
news.engineering_impact: The release separates 10,307 training tasks from the 500 tasks used for evaluation.
news.limitations: The rise from 0.8% to 21.2% was measured in simulation. The physical demonstration concerned one drawing.
news.evidence_status: Results reported by the developers include a simulation evaluation and a separate demonstration on a physical arm.
news.body:
Singapore lab Einsia AI released RoboUniverse-10K on November 25. It is a set of computer environments in which a program can move a robot arm and change the state of objects. The researchers tested whether extra training in these environments could help a model complete new tasks. On a separate set of 500 tasks, their model's success rate rose from 0.8% to 21.2% after training.

The team used recordings from physical robots as a starting point for deciding what objects and actions a task should contain. It turned these into interactive scenes, where the simulator updates what happens when an arm moves or touches an object. Of the 10,807 tasks, 10,307 are for training and 500 are held out for evaluation. During evaluation the software can observe and act through fixed interfaces. It cannot read hidden object coordinates or the rules used to check its work.

A separate demonstration ran the model on a physical Franka arm. Given an example image, the arm drew the Einsia logo on a whiteboard whose height had not been supplied in advance. Einsia says the model used observation, trial movements and correction. The 0.8% and 21.2% figures describe the simulated evaluation.

The authors kept the visual encoder and alignment modules fixed while updating the language backbone during fine-tuning. A comparison with another method needs to preserve the held-out tasks and specify what observations and actions each model can use.

news.title: Universal Robots moves 3D vision processing onto the robot controller
news.summary: Universal Robots and Inbolt showed in Nuremberg how Inbolt Standard locates parts on a Gen 7 robot controller. The camera plugs into the end of the arm, and the new setup removes the separate industrial computer formerly needed for that processing.
news.details: At SPS in Nuremberg on November 24, Universal Robots and Inbolt introduced an integration that runs 3D vision on the robot's controller. Inbolt Standard uses image and depth data to locate a part so the arm can bring its tool to the correct position. It now carries out that calculation on the CB7 Core controller. The companies scheduled a live demonstration on a Gen 7 arm at the November 24 to 26 show.
news.technical_novelty: The camera connects at the end of the arm, and the robot controller computes the part position.
news.engineering_impact: The setup removes the separate computer previously needed for this 3D vision processing.
news.limitations: The reported repeatability of 0.5 to 0.7 millimetres covers stationary parts.
news.evidence_status: The suppliers announced the integration and reported repeatability on stationary parts.
news.body:
At SPS in Nuremberg on November 24, Universal Robots and Inbolt introduced an integration that runs 3D vision on the robot's controller. Inbolt Standard uses image and depth data to locate a part so the arm can bring its tool to the correct position. It now carries out that calculation on the CB7 Core controller. The companies scheduled a live demonstration on a Gen 7 arm at the November 24 to 26 show.

An Orbbec camera uses the power and gigabit Ethernet connectors on the g-Series tool flange, the mount at the end of the arm. The camera signal travels through the robot. The previous setup needed an external industrial computer for vision processing. To configure a part, the system uses a file from computer-aided design describing its shape. The suppliers say configuration runs locally in under ten minutes and requires no collection or labeling of images.

The suppliers quote repeatability of 0.5 to 0.7 millimetres on fixed parts. Repeatability describes how closely repeated estimates agree under the stated conditions. It does not measure how close each estimate is to the true position. The release specifies PolyScope X 10.13 or later for three g-Series arms and describes an external camera cable for compatible older arms using a CB7 controller.

The integration changes both the route of the signal and where object localization runs. The stated repeatability covers stationary parts. The release gives no measurement for the same task with the part in motion.

news.title: Kawasaki and Beckhoff sign agreement on robot controls
news.summary: Kawasaki Heavy Industries and Beckhoff signed a memorandum of understanding at SPS in Nuremberg. They will explore using the EtherCAT industrial network and Beckhoff software in Kawasaki robot control systems.
news.details: On November 27, Kawasaki Heavy Industries and Germany's Beckhoff Automation announced a memorandum signed at the SPS trade show in Nuremberg. The partners want to make it easier to connect equipment from different vendors to Kawasaki industrial robots. The agreement covers exploring control technology that runs on industrial computers and discussing support and training for the people who assemble production systems.
news.technical_novelty: The partners will explore sending commands and measurements over an industrial network called EtherCAT.
news.engineering_impact: The work aims to make it easier to connect or replace equipment supplied by different manufacturers.
news.limitations: The partners have yet to publish a list of compatible devices or measurements of communication delay.
news.evidence_status: The partners confirmed the memorandum. Technical results are yet to be published.
news.organization: Kawasaki Heavy Industries and Beckhoff Automation
news.body:
On November 27, Kawasaki Heavy Industries and Germany's Beckhoff Automation announced a memorandum signed at the SPS trade show in Nuremberg. The partners want to make it easier to connect equipment from different vendors to Kawasaki industrial robots. The agreement covers exploring control technology that runs on industrial computers and discussing support and training for the people who assemble production systems.

EtherCAT is a network that carries commands and measurements between an industrial controller and attached devices. Kawasaki put the network at the centre of a controller concept shown in Tokyo in December 2025. The new agreement gives Kawasaki and Beckhoff a way to work on putting the concept into practice. They will also assess TwinCAT, Beckhoff's software for running automation from a computer.

A robot cell may contain a camera, sensors and software as well as the arm. If each connection has to be built separately, replacing a camera or adding another sensor becomes more work. The companies want equipment choices and later changes to be easier. They have also said they will discuss training and support for system integrators, the specialists who put those pieces together.

The release describes work on interfaces and tools. It gives no supported-device list or measured communication delays on a working line. Connection compatibility and control performance under load will need separate evidence.

news.title: XPENG plans to train its new humanoid in its own stores
news.summary: Chinese carmaker XPENG publicly showed its IRON humanoid at AI Day in Guangzhou. It plans to start training the robot as a store assistant in the first quarter of 2027.
news.details: XPENG presented its new IRON humanoid in Guangzhou on November 25. The carmaker wants to see how the machine can learn the role of a store assistant. It targets the first quarter of 2027 for training in its own shops and the second quarter for a public release. The AI Day announcement described the hardware and planned uses without giving results from work with shoppers.
news.technical_novelty: XPENG says the robot has 76 independent ways to move and more than 1,500 touch-sensing points.
news.engineering_impact: The company plans to use its own stores to train the robot as an assistant.
news.limitations: XPENG gave target dates for training and public release. It did not report results from helping shoppers.
news.evidence_status: Manufacturer launch announcement with target dates for training and public release.
news.body:
XPENG presented its new IRON humanoid in Guangzhou on November 25. The carmaker wants to see how the machine can learn the role of a store assistant. It targets the first quarter of 2027 for training in its own shops and the second quarter for a public release. The AI Day announcement described the hardware and planned uses without giving results from work with shoppers.

XPENG says IRON has 76 degrees of freedom, a count of independent ways its parts can move. It also reports more than 1,500 points that sense touch and says coverage exceeds 80% of key body areas. Three of the company's Turing chips run models on the robot and help control its body. XPENG built the systems for planning tasks, navigating and handling objects together with the robot’s hardware.

The company lists tasks created by voice or app, autonomous navigation and charging, and reporting of unusual conditions. It plans to use its own stores to train the assistant. Working in those shops would give the team real examples of the objects the robot needs to handle and the spaces it must move through.

The movement count and touch measurements describe the design. Assessing a store task will require success rates for the intended actions and evidence about how the machine responds when people enter its working area.

news.title: Progress delivers equipment for a robot experiment to the space station
news.summary: NASA confirmed that a Progress cargo spacecraft docked with the station’s Rassvet module on November 26. Kommersant reported that the cargo included cameras, a manipulator and integration equipment for a robot experiment intended to assist work outside the station.
news.details: On November 26, the Progress MS-36 cargo spacecraft docked with the International Space Station. NASA identifies the ship as Progress 97 and puts its docking at the Earth-facing port of Rassvet at 7:08 a.m. Eastern Standard Time. Kommersant reports that the cargo included cameras, a manipulator and integration equipment for Teledroid, a robot experiment aimed at assisting astronauts with work outside the station.
news.technical_novelty: In the experiment, a wearable device will relay the operator’s movements for the robot to reproduce.
news.engineering_impact: The cameras and arm are equipment for testing remote control on the station.
news.limitations: The docking reports document delivery and give no results from a session outside the station.
news.evidence_status: NASA confirmed docking. Kommersant reported the equipment, and TASS described the planned control method.
news.body:
On November 26, the Progress MS-36 cargo spacecraft docked with the International Space Station. NASA identifies the ship as Progress 97 and puts its docking at the Earth-facing port of Rassvet at 7:08 a.m. Eastern Standard Time. Kommersant reports that the cargo included cameras, a manipulator and integration equipment for Teledroid, a robot experiment aimed at assisting astronauts with work outside the station.

The spacecraft lifted off from Baikonur on November 24. The experiment calls for remote operation, with the robot reproducing motions made by an operator. TASS describes an operator wearing an exoskeleton, a device attached to the body that relays movements to the control system. The robot also uses machine vision to process camera images. Its design resembles an upper body without legs.

After delivery, the equipment has to be connected and the motion link checked. Operators need to know that a command reaches the robot and that they can see the result. The docking reports contain no measurements of those steps or of the robot's performance outside the station.

The cargo report documents delivery of components. Evaluation of remote operation will need measurements of command and feedback delay, together with the accuracy of the resulting motion in a defined task.

technology_signal.title: Part localisation moves to the robot controller
technology_signal.summary: The camera plugs into the Gen 7 tool flange. A CB7 Core controller computes part positions, replacing a separate computer for this task.
technology_signal.implications: The suppliers quote 0.5 to 0.7 mm repeatability on fixed parts. Moving parts require their own evaluation.
